subject: Private Endpoint Outbound Touchpoints & Firewall Policy Clarification
messages:
From: Tom Saito <tsaito@medsys.health>
To: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
Cc: security@medsys.health
Date: 2028-03-14T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Quick clarification on private runtime outbound dependencies

Rafael,

Thanks for the onboarding call yesterday. Our security team needs a concise mapping of exactly what outbound network endpoints a Private (VPC/on-prem) Redwood control plane and runtime will reach from our environment.

Specifically we need: 1) the list of IP addresses (or IP ranges) we should allow in our firewall for egress, 2) DNS names/FQDNs that are used (so we can permit FQDN-based rules), 3) ports/protocols, and 4) notes on whether Redwood uses stable IPs or rotates ephemeral egress IPs (and the rotation cadence).

Two extra constraints:
- We do TLS interception for outbound traffic in our egress stack; will SNI-based allowlisting be sufficient or do you require IP-level allowlisting?
- We need to know whether telemetry/usage/health pings go to the same control-plane endpoints or a separate telemetry pipeline.

Attached are the SOC2 evidence questions that triggered this (medsys-evidence-requests.pdf). If you can provide an Excel-style matrix that we can drop into our change ticket, that would be ideal.

Can you get this to us by end of day tomorrow (2028-03-15)?

Thanks,
Tom
Security Operations
MedSys Health

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Saito <tsaito@medsys.health>
Cc: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-03-14T13:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Quick clarification on private runtime outbound dependencies

Tom — thanks for the note and for attaching the SOC2 list. I put together a short outbound touchpoints matrix and an annotated checklist (attached: egress-touchpoints-raf-20280314.xlsx). High-level answers below; see the spreadsheet for the canonical allowlist entries you can paste into your firewall change.

Summary (short):
- Primary control-plane endpoints: *.control.redwood.ai (443/TCP) — we publish both FQDNs and a stable set of NAT egress CIDRs for customers who cannot do FQDN allowlisting.
- Telemetry and metrics: telemetry.ingest.redwood.ai (443/TCP) — same TLS termination but separate backend; you can treat it as a distinct FQDN for controls and monitoring.
- Ephemeral/worker egress (model hosts): model-exit.redwood.ai (443/TCP) — these are generally ephemeral and tied to the Dedicated/Private runtime; we provide a short-lived CIDR list and a lookup API for live operations.

Notes on your specific questions:
- SNI allowlisting: supported and recommended where you have TLS interception. We sign certificates with well-known CNs and support SNI stability. However, for customers doing deep packet inspection + outbound block policies, we still provide NAT egress CIDRs so you can whitelist by IP if you prefer.
- Rotation cadence: control-plane NAT CIDRs are stable across multi-month windows (we only add/remove during major infra changes and give 30 days notice). Model/worker egress IPs can rotate daily for autoscaling clusters; our lookup API returns a current set and a timestamp.
- Ports/protocols: primarily outbound HTTPS (443/TCP). A few health-checks use 80/TCP for legacy probes — these are optional and documented in the spreadsheet.

Action items I propose:
1) Use the attached spreadsheet to seed your firewall change ticket (there's a ready-to-copy column).
2) If you need strict IP-only rules, let us know and we'll enable an IP-pinned mode for your account and provide a time-limited allowlist export.
3) We can grant your security team read access to our IP lookup endpoint and a webhook for rotation events.

I looped in David from infra to add specifics on TLS/SNI caveats and the exact header fields we rely on when customers perform TLS inspection.

-Rafael
Product Security Liaison
Redwood Inference

Attachments: egress-touchpoints-raf-20280314.xlsx (xlsx)

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Saito <tsaito@medsys.health>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-03-15T08:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Quick clarification on private runtime outbound dependencies

Tom / Rafael — quick technical addendum on firewall rule patterns and TLS interception behavior we see in the field.

Firewall guidance (recommended order of preference):
1) FQDN + port allowlist (best for agility): Allow *.control.redwood.ai, telemetry.ingest.redwood.ai, model-exit.redwood.ai on 443/TCP. Edge cases: some older firewall appliances evaluate FQDN only at session start (not per-request), which is usually OK.
2) SNI-only allowlist: Works well with TLS interception; ensure your proxy preserves the SNI field to Redwood (we do not rely on behind-the-proxy client certificates for SNI routing).
3) IP/CIDR allowlist (strict): Use our published egress CIDRs (column: Published_Egress_CIDRs) and maintain a daily sync with our lookup API. This is the most robust against broken SNI or DNS rewriting but requires automation on your side for rotation events.

Protocol and port details:
- 443/TCP: Control plane, telemetry, model exit tunnels (mandatory).
- 80/TCP: Optional health-check endpoints used by bootstrap scripts; not required after initial setup.
- 53/UDP/TCP: DNS lookups — if you block DNS at the egress, ensure Redwood FQDNs resolve to the expected addresses (we publish DNS overrides for air-gapped installs).

TLS inspection caveats:
- Do not rewrite SNI. If your intercepting proxy re-writes SNI to an internal host, calls will be routed incorrectly. Preserve SNI and forward TLS client hello where possible.
- We support ALPN and expect h2 or http/1.1; allow both.
- For mTLS: Redwood control plane does not require customer mTLS by default, but we support mutual TLS for Private deployments under an enterprise agreement.

Operational hooks:
- IP lookup API: https://api.redwood.ai/v1/egress-cidrs?account=MSH-2028-RED-57 (read-only; returns current set + valid_until).
- Rotation webhook: we can send a signed POST to an endpoint you provide when the published CIDR set changes.

I'll also note one pragmatic pattern used by several regulated customers: use FQDN + SNI in normal operations, and implement a nightly automation job that calls our lookup API and auto-updates firewall CIDRs if your appliance supports it. That gives both the operational simplicity of FQDNs and the safety of IP-level enforcement for audit windows.

-David
Principal Infrastructure Engineer
Redwood Inference
